svg.title: Where the effort really goes in a security project, and the five questions that make default deny operable
svg.desc: Top: a bar split 30 percent buy and configure against 70 percent process change. The 70 percent is broken into the items that actually consume the schedule: the printer that cannot authenticate, the medical device vendor who refuses to cooperate, visitor and contractor access, the fallback path for when the authentication server is unreachable, and the question of who is on call at two in the morning. Middle: the whitelist ownership flow in five steps, each with a named owner and a time budget - business submits with a business case, security approves or rejects within two days, network implements within one day, the rule is registered with an expiry date, and the owner reviews and removes it when the project ends. Bottom: the two failure modes, an approval queue so long that teams route around the firewall, and rules with no expiry date that accumulate until nobody can read the policy.
svg.text: The budget line is 30 percent. The schedule line is 70 percent, and it is not IT's to control.
This is why security projects that were "technically complete in week two" ship in month seven.
what happens when the auth server is down,
and who answers at 02:00 when it is
"fail open" is a decision, not an accident
DEFAULT DENY IS OPERABLE ONLY IF THESE FIVE ARE ANSWERED
two days, or teams route around you
and a log entry tying rule to ticket
a rule without expiry is forever
an approval queue so slow that teams build a tunnel to somewhere else - the policy is intact and unenforced
and rules nobody dares delete: after three years, the whitelist is a list of former projects and nobody can tell a business need from an archaeology find.
The design document should contain the approval service level and the expiry policy alongside the firewall specification. One without the other is unenforceable in practice.
Measure it: the median time from submit to working flow, and the number of rules older than their owning project. Both numbers predict whether the policy survives.
A security control that the business cannot obtain legally will be obtained illegally, with a 4G modem and a personal hotspot.
